title: Constitutional Law Basics
summary: Understand how constitutions work in Africa: constitutional supremacy and the rule of law, separation of powers, bills of rights and limitations, courts and judicial review, federal, unitary and devolved systems and amendment, and how citizens use the constitution.
audience: Students, civil servants, journalists, activists and citizens who want to understand their constitution

body.p: A constitution is the supreme law of a country. It sets up the main institutions of government, divides power between them, states how leaders are chosen and removed, and protects the rights of the people. Most African countries adopted written constitutions at independence, and many were rewritten during the democratic reforms of the 1990s and later, such as South Africa's Constitution of 1996 and Kenya's Constitution of 2010.

Under constitutional supremacy, any law or government action that conflicts with the constitution is invalid to the extent of the conflict. This differs from parliamentary sovereignty, the traditional British idea that parliament can make or unmake any law. Most modern African constitutions declare themselves supreme.

list: Constitutionalism means government is limited by law, not just that a constitution exists.
The rule of law means everyone, including leaders, is subject to the law, and laws are applied fairly and predictably.
A constitution can only be legitimate and durable if people accept it; many countries used public consultations to draft theirs.

body.tip: Read the preamble and founding provisions of your own constitution; they state the values that courts use to interpret the rest.

body.p: Government power is divided among three branches so that no single person or body holds unchecked power.

list: The legislature (parliament or national assembly) makes laws, approves budgets and oversees the executive.
The executive (president or prime minister and cabinet, and the public service) implements laws and runs government.
The judiciary (the courts) interprets the law and resolves disputes, including disputes about the constitution.

body.p: Each branch limits the others. Parliament can question ministers, reject bills and, in many countries, impeach a president. The president may veto or refer bills back. Courts can strike down unconstitutional laws and actions. Independent bodies such as electoral commissions, auditors-general, human rights commissions and public protectors or ombudsmen add further checks.

In presidential systems, such as those of Nigeria, Kenya and Ghana, the president is directly elected and heads the executive. In parliamentary systems, the head of government comes from and answers to parliament; South Africa is a hybrid in which parliament elects the president.

body.tip: Judicial independence (secure tenure, fair appointment and protected salaries for judges) is what makes checks by the courts real.

body.p: Most constitutions include a bill of rights that protects individuals against abuse of state power and, increasingly, requires the state to provide basic services.

list: Civil and political rights: life, dignity, equality, freedom of expression, assembly, association and religion, a fair trial and the right to vote.
Socio-economic rights: access to housing, health care, food, water, education and social security, often to be realised progressively within available resources.
Environmental rights and rights of children, women, persons with disabilities and minorities.

body.p: Few rights are absolute. Constitutions usually allow limitations only by a law of general application that is reasonable and justifiable in an open and democratic society, considering factors such as the importance of the purpose and whether less restrictive means exist. Some rights, such as freedom from torture, are usually treated as non-derogable.

body.tip: When analysing a rights problem, ask: is a right limited, and if so, is the limitation justified?

body.p: Judicial review is the power of courts to declare laws and government actions unconstitutional. Many countries have a constitutional court or a supreme court with final say on constitutional questions.

list: In 2017, Kenya's Supreme Court annulled a presidential election result because of irregularities and ordered a fresh election.
In 2020, Malawi's Constitutional Court annulled the 2019 presidential election; a rerun was held later that year.
South Africa's Constitutional Court has ruled on issues including the death penalty, access to HIV treatment and the accountability of the executive to parliament.

body.p: Modern constitutions often widen standing, so people can bring cases in the public interest, not only for themselves. Remedies include declaring a law invalid, ordering government to act, and awarding compensation. Courts must still respect the role of the other branches and avoid making policy themselves.

body.tip: Court judgments are usually published free online; reading the summary first makes long judgments easier to follow.

list: Federal systems divide power between national and state governments, each with its own constitution-based powers. Nigeria and Ethiopia are federal.
Unitary systems concentrate power at the centre, which may delegate some functions to local government. Ghana is unitary.
Devolved systems give counties or provinces substantial constitutional powers within a unitary state. Kenya devolved significant functions and funds to 47 counties in 2010.

body.p: Constitutions are harder to change than ordinary laws. Amendments may need a special majority of parliament, such as two-thirds of members (267 of 400 seats) or, for core provisions, three-quarters (300 of 400), and sometimes approval in a referendum. Debates over amendments to remove presidential term limits have been major political issues in several African countries.
Some courts have held that certain basic features of a constitution cannot be removed even by amendment.

body.tip: Check which sections of your constitution are entrenched and what majority is needed to change them.

body.p: Constitutions are not only for lawyers. They work best when citizens know them, use them and defend them.

list: Vote and take part in public consultations on laws and budgets; many constitutions require public participation.
Use access-to-information laws to request government records.
Petition parliament or local councils about problems.
Approach independent bodies, such as human rights commissions and public protectors or ombudsmen, with complaints.
Join civic organisations that monitor government and educate communities.
Respect the rights of others; constitutional rights carry responsibilities too.

body.p: Regional bodies also matter: the African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance commits African Union members to democratic principles, and the AU can suspend members after unconstitutional changes of government.

body.tip: Keep a copy of your constitution on your phone; many governments publish it free online in several languages.
